title: Paul in Athens (Acts 17:16–34)
hookLine: he quotes their own poets: in him we live and move and have our being

cards: Where do you start with someone who sees the world differently, at a wedding or in a comment thread? Most of us start with where they're wrong.

Paul is in Athens, the ancient world's city of ideas, alone, waiting for his friends. He walks the streets, deeply stirred: the city is full of statues and altars to many gods, and he's a Jew who worships one.
He talks in the synagogue and the marketplace with anyone who'll listen, Stoic and Epicurean philosophers among them. Some call him a babbler. Others are curious.
They take him to the Areopagus, the council's hill, and say: tell us this new thing.

teach.b: Paul begins with a compliment: I see you're a very religious people. Walking around, he says, I found an altar inscribed, in the King James Bible: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD."

teach.h: HE STARTS FROM WHAT THEY HAVE.
teach.b: He doesn't mock it; he starts from it. The one you honor without knowing is the one I proclaim: the God who made the world, who doesn't live in buildings made by hands, and isn't far from any of us.

Then, unexpectedly for a traveling Jewish teacher, he quotes their own poets: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring."
The second line is from the Greek poet Aratus, about three centuries earlier; the first is often credited to another, Epimenides, though scholars aren't sure.
Either way, Paul stands on their hill and speaks their language. Then he reaches his center: a day of judgment, and a man raised from the dead.
That's where the room splits: at the resurrection, some laugh. Others say, politely, we'll hear you again. A few believe, and Luke names two: Dionysius, a council member, and a woman, Damaris.
Christians have long pointed to this speech as a way to talk across a gap: start with what's good and true in the other person's world, honor it, then say plainly what you believe.
A line Paul borrowed from Greek poets has been prayed and sung by Christians ever since.

teach.h: IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE.

how: Christians often point to Paul's speech on the Areopagus as a model for speaking respectfully with people of other views. The line 'in him we live, and move, and have our being' is widely used in prayers and hymns.

o: a foreign god the Athenians had banned
a god nobody had ever worshiped before
a god honored at an altar without a name

p: the hill where the council met

he begins by noting they're very religious, and starts from their altar to the unknown god.

games.q: you're Paul, standing before the thinkers of Athens, in a city full of altars to many gods. how do you begin?
o: point to their altar to an unknown god and start there.
stay silent and let them ask questions.
games.why: he begins with their own altar, to the unknown god, and quotes their own poets: in him we live, and move, and have our being.

practice: Picture someone with a view you don't share, a politics, a faith, a way of raising kids or spending money, and look for their altar to the unknown god: the thing they're reaching for that you can honor, like safety, fairness, freedom, or love for their family.
Name it kindly; you don't have to agree, just find the good. If you pray, you can pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Unknown god. The inscription Paul found on an altar in Athens, which he used to introduce the God he'd come to tell them about.
